routes.description: Establish that Paul understood Jesus as an earthly historical person by combining Pauline biographical and familial references with an earthly reading of the crucifying rulers and corroboration from sources connected to Paul and the Gospel tradition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the Pauline references are best explained as ordinary historical claims, the rulers passage situates the crucifixion among human authorities, and the proposed Acts and Gospel corroboration remains sufficiently independent and reliable to reinforce that reading.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative evidence is better explained by Paul referring to a human Jesus who lived and was crucified on Earth than by a wholly celestial setting for the saving events.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline references to ancestry, birth, teachings, associates, betrayal, and execution supply meaningful historical particularity.
Establish from the context of First Corinthians that the rulers responsible for the crucifixion are human authorities, even if spiritual forces also participated.
Show that references to James and other brothers of the Lord are most coherently understood as biological relationships to Jesus.
Establish that Acts is substantially reliable and connected to a companion of Paul, making its historical Jesus relevant to reconstructing Paul's understanding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a sufficiently broad Pauline corpus so that relevant historical references are not excluded solely by disputed authorship judgments.
Show that dispersed incidental correspondences among Gospel narratives are more expected on historical information than deliberate literary harmonization.

routes.description: Establish that Paul's accepted letters do not securely locate Jesus's ministry, death, and resurrection on Earth, while their cosmic language permits a flesh-bearing celestial figure killed by demonic rulers in a mythic heavenly realm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline biographical and familial expressions remain materially ambiguous, the rulers and cosmology make a heavenly crucifixion viable, and Acts and Gospel narratives cannot independently import a later earthly biography into Paul's letters.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest relevant Pauline evidence remains compatible with, and materially supports, a mortal embodied Jesus whose death and resurrection occurred in a celestial rather than terrestrial realm.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the accepted Pauline letters lack an unambiguous earthly ministry or terrestrial location for Jesus's death and resurrection.
Show that the rulers of the age can be celestial demonic powers and that their concealed knowledge and interests fit that interpretation.
Establish that ancient cosmology allowed heavenly counterparts of earthly places, objects, and practices, making a celestial crucifixion intelligible.
Show that Acts and the Gospels are too disputed, literary, dependent, or historically unstable to determine what Paul believed about Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Pauline brother-of-the-Lord language can identify an ordinary baptized Christian rather than a biological sibling of Jesus.
Supply the comparative possibility that a savior cult could later place a nonhistorical divine figure into an earthly narrative.

sections.title: Pauline Biography, Silence, and Corpus Scope
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether the relevant Pauline letters contain historical markers sufficient to locate Jesus on Earth, and whether the admissible Pauline corpus expands or restricts that evidence.

sections.title: The Rulers and the Realm of Crucifixion
sections.rationale: The identity of the rulers of the age and the cosmological intelligibility of heavenly counterparts directly distinguish an earthly execution by human authorities from a celestial passion involving demonic powers.

sections.title: James and the Brothers of the Lord
sections.rationale: Whether Paul's references identify biological relatives or members of a baptized cultic family is among the most direct disputes over historical particularity within the Pauline evidence.

sections.title: Acts, Pauline Chronology, and Companion Authorship
sections.rationale: Acts can connect Paul to a thoroughly historical Jesus only if its chronology, factual reliability, first-person narration, and claimed relationship to a Pauline companion survive the competing literary explanation.

sections.title: Gospel Independence and Undesigned Coincidences
sections.rationale: The evidential value of cross-Gospel correspondences depends on whether dispersed details reflect independent historical information or deliberate adaptation and harmonization of earlier narrative sources.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Carrier's mythicist thesis grants that Paul conceived Jesus as acquiring mortal Jewish flesh while locating his death and resurrection in a mythic realm rather than on Earth.
moves.attributionBasis: The proposition occurs within Carrier's uninterrupted thesis-setting turn after the moderator explicitly invites him to present his position.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the celestial-mythic thesis and directly supplies the con route's proposed account of embodiment and location.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the thesis that subsequent arguments are intended to support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim clearly distinguishes mortal Jewish embodiment from the proposed nonterrestrial location of death and resurrection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a definition of the version of mythicism being defended, the categorical formulation matches its limited thesis-setting function.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between bodily mortality and terrestrial location is coherent, though the excerpt does not yet explain the realm's mechanics.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move states the thesis precisely but offers only a brief savior-cult analogy rather than developed support for its historical probability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the con motion-level account of Jesus as embodied yet killed outside the terrestrial realm.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move defines Carrier's own thesis and does not materially interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier expressly grants flesh, blood, Jewish identity, mortality, and death while locating the events in a mythic realm rather than Jerusalem or Earth.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The seven accepted Pauline letters do not locate Jesus's life and death on Earth or describe an earthly ministry, while presenting his teachings as received through revelation.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier remains the sole speaker throughout the passage and explicitly turns from comparative religion to the evidentiary contents of Paul's letters.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the con route's central evidentiary argument from what the accepted Pauline letters do and do not say.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents a specific textual pattern directly tied to a central route bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The listed silences are pertinent, but the inference from omitted biography to a nonterrestrial setting needs genre and expectation comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The observations can support ambiguity, but a material bridge remains from epistolary silence and revelatory teaching to celestial location.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete categories of omission are identified, while representativeness and expected Pauline reporting remain insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central bridge concerning the absence of unambiguous terrestrial biography in accepted letters.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt develops an affirmative silence argument without expressly characterizing a developed opposing explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier lists no pre-death meetings, disciple selection, ministry, miracles, exorcisms, or other earthly activity and contrasts these absences with revelation.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The restriction of Pauline evidence to seven letters rests on a contestable authorship consensus, and the case for treating all thirteen letters as Pauline should be reconsidered.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion to McLatchie, who identifies Carrier by name, cites Carrier's methodological concern, and states his contrary authorship position.

components.text: Whether the seven accepted letters themselves lack an unambiguous earthly ministry or terrestrial death location.
Whether restricting the evidentiary corpus to seven letters is methodologically justified.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the secondary corpus premise but not the decisive textual-silence component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The authorship challenge is recoverable, though the evidentiary standard for reconsidering all thirteen letters remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the consensus as contestable rather than disproved, appropriately limiting the force of its methodological objection.

charity.alternative: A defensible critical consensus may still restrict secure Pauline evidence to seven letters.
charity.decisiveQualification: Carrier's quoted criticism of consensus formation does not itself authenticate all thirteen letters.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Paul's letters contain multiple historical markers for Jesus, including Davidic descent, birth from a woman under the law, teachings, brothers, followers, betrayal, a final meal, and crucifixion by rulers.

components.text: Whether Pauline letters contain meaningful biographical particulars bearing on an earthly Jesus.
Whether mortal embodiment and the cited biographical markers are compatible with a wholly nonterrestrial saving career.
Whether every cited marker comes from the securely accepted seven-letter corpus.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's rulers of this age can be demonic powers, whose hostile motives and ignorance of God's concealed salvific plan fit the crucifixion passage better than obedient earthly authorities.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie explicitly yields the cited passage to Carrier, whose ensuing uninterrupted turn analyzes the Greek terminology and contrasts possible agents of the crucifixion.

components.text: Whether the rulers who crucified Jesus provide a secure human and terrestrial biographical marker.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly attacks the inference from rulers to human terrestrial execution and supplies the defeating consequence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the human reading but materially compresses its strongest qualification concerning exceptional or corrupt authorities.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier contrasts Romans 13 obedience with agents attempting to thwart a concealed cosmic plan and argues that this incongruity favors demonic rulers.

moves.proposition: Ancient Jewish cosmology could place counterparts of earthly objects and practices in heavenly realms, making a celestial counterpart of crucifixion intelligible within that worldview.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The surrounding contrast between divine wisdom and ordinary human wisdom indicates that the rulers who crucified Jesus in First Corinthians are human authorities rather than exclusively demonic forces.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly engages the decisive contextual inference about the rulers' identity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues for the more likely contextual reading without claiming that spiritual participation is impossible.

charity.decisiveQualification: The immediate chapters repeatedly contrast divine wisdom with human sages, debaters, and worldly status.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The context of First Corinthians 2 concerns human authorities, so its rulers can be understood as human even if demonic forces also participated spiritually in the crucifixion.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the exchange to Jonathan, whose sustained first-person response continues through the contextual conclusion.

components.text: Whether demonic participation requires construing the named rulers as exclusively spiritual agents.
Whether spiritual participation requires relocating the crucifixion itself to a heavenly realm.

response.rationale: The move directly distinguishes the grammatical identity of the rulers from possible spiritual participation, answering both exclusive-demonic identity and heavenly-location inferences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it expressly contacts the decisive inference and supplies a clear mixed-agency distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: Human identity, possible demonic participation, and terrestrial governing authority are carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The qualified formulation matches the contextual support and avoids claiming that spiritual agency is absent.

charity.alternative: Demonic forces may participate in or motivate the crucifixion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such participation does not entail that Paul's grammatical rulers are nonhuman or that the event is celestial.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Because Paul treats baptized Christians as the Lord's brethren, his title for James can identify a non-apostolic baptized Christian rather than a biological sibling of Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Richard by name, and the ensuing extended answer presents Carrier's book-based grammatical and contextual interpretation.

components.text: Whether references to James and brothers of the Lord provide unambiguous biological particularity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive inference from brother language to biological siblinghood.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among apostle, ordinary Christian, cultic brother, and biological brother is expressly drawn.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Carrier concludes that the usage is unclear rather than asserting that the cultic interpretation is conclusively established.

charity.alternative: The marked phrase brother of the Lord may identify Jesus's biological sibling rather than any baptized Christian.
charity.decisiveQualification: General Christian brotherhood does not automatically explain the marked title attached specifically to James.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Pauline cultic kinship establishes a live alternative, though the bridge from general brethren to this marked title remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The firstborn-among-brethren concept supports possibility, but comparative Pauline usage of the exact construction is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary cultic-brother-language bridge with a specific Pauline rationale.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The combined references to James, the brothers of the Lord, and Jesus's mother alongside his brothers support a biological rather than merely cultic relationship.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the biological-sibling question to Jonathan, and the answer advances his interpretation across Pauline, Gospel, and Acts references.

components.text: Whether the brother terminology is better explained as cultic membership than biological kinship.
Whether familial references provide historical particularity for an earthly Jesus.

response.rationale: The move answers the cultic reading by combining James with Gospel and Acts family groupings, though the later-source independence needed for convergence is not fully defended.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive biological-versus-cultic issue but compresses the independence objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The biological inference is clear, but Pauline evidence and later narrative traditions are combined without an explicit independence qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Mention beside Jesus's mother supports biological kinship, but later-source dependence limits what it establishes about Paul's usage.

charity.alternative: Paul's usage may be cultic, while later narratives independently develop a biological family tradition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Later mother-and-brothers groupings do not by themselves determine the meaning of Paul's earlier phrase.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The convergence is coherent if the sources are evidentially linked, but that independence and transmission bridge remains material.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central familial-reference bridge, though part of the support comes from later sources.

moves.evidenceBasis: McLatchie combines Paul's James and brothers language with Matthew's named brothers and Acts's grouping of Jesus's mother alongside the brothers.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: First Corinthians 9 remains compatible with cultic brethren, while later Gospel and Acts family traditions cannot resolve Paul's ambiguous usage because Paul shows no awareness of those stories.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly returns to Richard, whose answer addresses both the Pauline passage and McLatchie's appeal to later narrative sources.

components.text: Whether later Gospel and Acts family traditions can determine the meaning of Paul's earlier ambiguous terminology.
Whether First Corinthians 9 independently requires biological brothers.

response.rationale: Carrier identifies the source-separation failure in the convergence argument and states that later legends cannot resolve Paul absent evidence that Paul knew those stories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies the independence defect and its consequence for the proposed convergence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between Paul's usage and later narrative family traditions is clearly delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Source separation is a strong limitation, though calling the later material legends assumes more than the excerpt demonstrates.

charity.alternative: Later traditions might preserve authentic family information that clarifies Paul's compressed reference.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preservation remains possible even if direct Pauline awareness of the written Gospel stories is absent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-separation objection validly blocks using later narratives as straightforward evidence of Paul's intended meaning.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's apparent lack of Gospel-story awareness is pertinent, but the excerpt does not exclude common earlier tradition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central later-source-independence bridge and attacks familial convergence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly emphasizes independence but somewhat compresses the possibility of a shared earlier family tradition.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier maintains that First Corinthians 9 remains unclear and that later Gospel family stories cannot establish Paul's meaning because Paul shows no awareness of them.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Acts is an agenda-driven work of fictionalized history that may reshape source material so extensively that historical facts cannot reliably be separated from its narrative embellishments.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Richard for his account of Acts, and Carrier gives a sustained description of its author, aims, literary method, and possible source use.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive move describes a literary model without yet engaging a developed opposing reliability case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier characterizes Acts as moral, political, and theological fictionalized history whose possible source facts are difficult to separate from embellishment and change.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Undesigned correspondences between Paul's letters and Acts support Acts's substantial historical accuracy and the identification of its author as Paul's traveling companion Luke.

components.text: Whether Acts's narrative is so freely fictionalized that substantial historical accuracy cannot be recovered.
Whether Acts possesses sufficient independence to corroborate Pauline-era historical claims.
